items.title: AI-Based Solar Power Forecasting and Health Monitoring Techniques: Recent Trends and Challenges
items.abstract: Solar energy has emerged as one of the most promising renewable energy sources due to its sustainability, abundance, and environmental benefits. However, the intermittent nature of solar power generation and system reliability challenges necessitate accurate forecasting and effective health monitoring techniques. Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), has significantly transformed solar energy systems by improving forecasting accuracy, fault detection, predictive maintenance, and energy storage optimization. This review paper explores recent advancements in AI-based solar power forecasting and health monitoring techniques, emphasizing models such as Support Vector Machine (SVM), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and hybrid frameworks. The study also examines AI-driven predictive maintenance approaches, including IoT-based monitoring, digital twin technologies, and thermal imaging methods for photovoltaic systems and battery energy storage systems. Furthermore, recent trends such as explainable AI, reinforcement learning, and smart grid integration are discussed. The paper highlights key challenges, including data quality, computational complexity, model generalization, and real-time deployment, while identifying future opportunities for intelligent and scalable solar energy management systems.

items.title: AI-Driven Cybersecurity and Digital Trust in Next-Generation Travel Management Systems
items.abstract: The travel and aviation industry has evolved from paper-based, isolated booking systems into a cloud-enabled, AI-driven ecosystem processing billions of passenger transactions each year. While this digital transformation has improved operational efficiency and customer experience, it has also expanded the industry's cyberattack surface, exposing airlines, online travel agencies, payment providers, and airport authorities to fraud, ransomware, identity theft, and other data-driven threats. This chapter examines how artificial intelligence and blockchain-based identity frameworks collectively strengthen digital trust and reshape travel management. It traces the transition from centralized Global Distribution Systems to hybrid API-based architectures and from Web 2.0 identity silos to Web 3.0 self-sovereign identity. It concludes by highlighting emerging risks associated with generative AI and hybrid distribution ecosystems, alongside governance strategies for building resilient, future-ready travel infrastructures.

items.title: AI-Driven Modeling and Simulation of Smart Microgrids
items.abstract: The decentralization, digitization, and decarbonization of energy systems have brought smart microgrids to the center of attention as we look at the modern power network. These local energy systems integrate distributed energy resources (DERs), energy storage, and advanced control techniques to develop reliability, resilience, and sustainability. However, these nonlinearities, complexity, and stochastic properties inherent in a smart microgrid are natural but demand more machine-like, adaptive modeling and simulation than is possible through rule-based models. Artificial intelligence (AI) has been added as the technology that turns out to address the challenges posed by the design, operation, and optimization of microgrids. Leveraging the strength of data-driven techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning, it is possible to use AI in order to construct dynamic, scalable, and predictive models that have the potential to be learnt either on the basis of historical or real-time data. Not only it is possible for such models to enhance the checking of the accuracy of the simulation, but they also help in making smart decisions regarding the prediction of loads, renewable integration, as well as fault identification and energy management systems. In this chapter, the authors&s; discussion focuses on AI-based approaches to smart microgrid model demonstration and simulation. It discusses significant AI strategies, simulation systems, and practical uses, as well as how AI can assist microgrids to be adaptive and independent in control under various conditions. Challenges and mitigation measures, the means of verification, and the prospects of integrating digital twins and multi-agent systems in order to render microgrids even more intelligent are also addressed. As the permeation of smart grids increases, one can expect modeling based on AI to potentially become a pillar of efficient, resilient, and sustainable power systems.

items.abstract: Phishing email remains a persistent cybersecurity threat, and large language models (LLMs) now allow fluent phishing text tobe produced at scale. This paper is a focused, literature-based comparative review of three recent studies that approach phishing emaildetection from different directions: a soft-voting ensemble with explainable-AI error analysis, a TF-IDF/SVM web platform with LIMEexplanations, and a stylometric classifier evaluated on GPT-4o-generated phishing emails alongside commercial spam filters. The studiesare compared by objective, dataset, feature family, model, evaluation protocol, reported metrics, explainability and stated limitations.Because the studies use different corpora and protocols, their reported figures are presented with attribution and are not ranked. Thecomparison suggests that content/structural detectors and stylometric detectors have been evaluated on largely disjoint data, so whethereither generalizes across conventional and AI-generated phishing is an open question raised by this review, not a verified research gap.The paper proposes a conceptual, unvalidated workflow that combines header/content/URL features, stylometric features, an ensembleclassifier and LIME-based analyst review, and specifies a future experimental protocol with hypotheses, cross-dataset tests and ablations.No new experimental results are reported.

items.title: AI-driven virtual influencers and the making of unequal digital livelihoods in Indonesia
items.abstract: Discussions about artificial intelligence in development often overlook how it reshapes everyday livelihoods in the Global South. This study examines how AI-driven virtual influencers (VIs) are transforming creative labour and digital visibility in Indonesia’s platform economy. Rather than autonomous technologies, VIs are produced through human–algorithm coordination shaped by platform logics and commercial imperatives. Drawing on 13 in-depth interviews with human influencers and one VI developer, this study shows how the expansion of VIs intensifies competition and creates increasing pressure for creators working with limited economic resources, unstable income, and self-funded production conditions. Thus, AI-driven systems reconfigure how income, visibility, and opportunities are distributed, contributing to unequal digital livelihoods. Simultaneously, VIs are designed to reflect local moral and aesthetic norms, revealing how global AI systems produce context-specific forms of inclusion and exclusion. These findings call for protection of creative workers, fair platform governance, and locally grounded AI policies.

items.title: AI-DRIVEN, EVIDENCE-BASED GENERATIVE DESIGN: A TEACHING FRAMEWORK FOR LANDSCAPE ARCHITECTONICS INTEGRATING RESEARCH FINDINGS, DESIGN PRECEDENTS, AND INTELLIGENT RECOGNITION AND JUDGMENT
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered design courses, but its use often stops at tool operation. Taking Landscape Architectonics, an undergraduate course in landscape architecture programs, as the vehicle, this paper builds a teaching framework for generative design that integrates four elements: research findings, design precedents, AI-based recognition and judgment, and AI generation. The core claim is simple. Teaching students to “use AI” means teaching them to run an evidence-constrained generative design chain. “AI-driven” therefore carries two meanings: at the tool level, AI executes generation; at the teaching level, evidence steers generation, and the work of teaching lies in leading students from the former toward the latter. Among the four elements, research findings and design precedents are static knowledge that travels across sites. Research findings supply criteria for what counts as good. Design precedents supply examples of what to do, distilled from 13 street design guidelines into 114 retrievable situation packages. AI-based recognition and AI generation produce dynamic outputs anchored to a specific site. Students mobilize these elements through three stages—reading the site, grounding the context, and giving form—and a chain of evidence disciplines each stage. The framework follows three design principles: complementary elements, partial embedding, and explicit judgment. Three classroom examples show how the framework operates. This paper focuses on framework construction and does not report learning-outcome data.

items.title: AI-Enabled Digital Forensics and Cybersecurity
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence and security have motivated digital forensics and the paradigm shift in the form of threat identification. This chapter views AI solutions such as neural networks and deep learning as powerful tools for detecting, analysing and reducing cyber threats. The AI has significantly changed the traditional methods of security, namely, enabling the existence of real-time threat intelligence, automated incident response, and predictive analytics. However, this new technology has several problems, including adversarial attacks, explainability concerns, and ethical concerns. By discussing in detail the ambivalent nature of AI in cybersecurity as both an effective defensive mechanism and a potential attack source, the chapter considers both sources of current research and real-world use. Topics of application that are discussed are relevant, including locating malware, intrusion-finding systems, preventing phishing, and digital forensics. New developments such as generative AI, explainable AI, and quantum-resistant security are also discussed in the chapter. It further discusses the significance of balanced development, ensuring that the security solutions of the future digital infrastructure are robust, transparent, and virtuous, controlled by AI.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence promises to improve drilling decisions, but field deployment remains constrained by delayed measurements, uncertain geology, inconsistent data quality and safety-critical operating limits. This critical review examines how measurement-while-drilling and logging while drilling information can support drilling rate optimisation adaptive well planning and predictive wellbore risk management within Saudi oil and gas operations. Thirty peer-reviewed publications issued between 2020 and 2025 were assessed through a structured, question led synthesis.The evidence was organized around measurement integrity, formation interpretation, optimisation architecture, trajectory revision, hazard prediction and deployment assurance. Published studies demonstrate substantial progress in rate - of - penetration forecasting, activity-aware influx detection and integrated geological-engineering planning. Nevertheless, model performance is generally assessed within particular fields or datasets; prospective validation, uncertainty calibration and evidence of avoided incidents remain less developed. The review proposes a bounded, human-supervised decision architecture in which physics-based constraints, data-quality controls and explicit operational authorisation separate algorithmic recommendations from drilling actions.

items.title: AI-Generated Fashion Imagery and Consumer Purchase Intention
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is widely adopted in fashion visual communication, yet imagery over-optimization causes product-image discrepancies and undermines consumer decisions. This study deconstructs three core characteristics of artificial intelligence-generated fashion imagery—visual realism, detail completeness, and style compatibility—and tests their impact on purchase intention via perceived authenticity and trust, with product price and consumer heterogeneity as moderators. Using a mixed-method approach (N = 845) and structural equation modeling, results confirm (1) the three characteristics positively influence purchase intention through direct risk reduction and indirect value identification, (2) trust plays dual mediating roles (direct and serial: artificial intelligence imagery → authenticity → trust → purchase intention), and (3) trust's mediation strengthens with higher prices (66.0% for high-price versus 39.6% for low-price products), and consumer segments differ in trust-building paths. This research enriches decision support system literature and offers actionable strategies for fashion brands.

items.title: AI-generated high-intensity interval training information: a cross-sectional comparative evaluation of quality and readability
items.abstract: Background AI chatbots are increasingly used for health and exercise information. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a common exercise topic, yet the quality, transparency, and readability of chatbot-generated HIIT information have not been systematically compared under a standardized testing protocol. Objective To compare selected dimensions of quality, transparency, and readability in HIIT-related responses generated by ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, and Perplexity, and to evaluate readability against a prespecified sixth-grade benchmark for public-facing health information. Methods This cross-sectional comparative content analysis was conducted in August 2026. Google Trends was used to identify HIIT-related search terms worldwide over the preceding 5 years. Of 29 candidate terms, 14 were retained after predefined screening, and each term was submitted once to each of four chatbots, yielding 56 responses. Two reviewers, both holding doctoral degrees in sports science, independently evaluated all responses using DISCERN, EQIP, the JAMA benchmark criteria, and GQS, which assessed complementary dimensions of information quality, usability, transparency, and overall usefulness. Inter-rater reliability was assessed before adjudication. Six readability indices were calculated. Because the same 14 queries were evaluated across all four chatbots, overall differences were tested using Friedman tests; significant results were followed by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. Kendall’s W was reported as the overall effect-size measure. Results Perplexity-generated responses had the highest median scores for DISCERN [51.50 (47.50, 53.75)], EQIP [75.00 (70.00, 80.00)], JAMA [1.00 (1.00, 1.00)], and GQS [4.00 (4.00, 4.00)]. Friedman tests showed significant differences across chatbots for DISCERN (χ 2 = 27.98, p < 0.001, W = 0.666), EQIP (χ 2 = 25.74, p < 0.001, W = 0.613), JAMA (χ 2 = 35.40, p < 0.001, W = 0.843), and GQS (χ 2 = 21.15, p < 0.001, W = 0.504). None of the four chatbots met the prespecified sixth-grade readability benchmark across the evaluated indices. Conclusion Under this specific testing protocol, HIIT-related responses generated by the four chatbots differed in the evaluated dimensions of information quality and transparency, with Perplexity-generated responses receiving higher median scores on all four assessment instruments. These scores should not be interpreted as direct evidence of factual accuracy, citation accuracy, or clinical safety, which were not independently assessed. None of the evaluated chatbot-generated responses met the prespecified readability benchmark.

items.title: AI-guided optimization and cradle-to-gate sustainability assessment of eco-friendly UHPC with supplementary cementitious materials and nano-additives
items.abstract: This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence (AI)-guided framework for predicting compressive strength (CS) and assessing the sustainability of ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) mixtures incorporating supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs), nano-additives, and sustainable waste-derived constituents. A database containing 1990 experimental records of 28-day CS was compiled from the literature. Three tree-based machine learning algorithms, namely Extra Trees Regressor (ETR), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGB), and Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM), together with stacked ensemble models, were developed and optimized using the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA). Based on outcomes, among all developed models, the SM-4 (XGB+ETR+LGBM) model achieved the best overall testing performance with an R² of 0.885, RMSE of 12.40 MPa, MAE of 8.80 MPa, MAPE of 5.94%, and RMSRE of 8.37%. SHAP analyses identified curing temperature, fiber dosage, silica fume content, cement dosage, and water content as the most influential predictors. Cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA)-based analyses further evaluated carbon emissions, embodied energy, and material cost. Additionally, a multi-objective inverse-design framework coupled the best-performing stacked model with NSGA-II and TOPSIS to identify UHPC mixture proportions for eight CS targets from 130 to 200 MPa while considering sustainability indicators and mixture-design requirements. Selected mixtures were produced and experimentally tested to compare measured CS with predictions and prescribed targets. Finally, an AI-guided graphical user interface (GUI) was developed for rapid CS prediction and sustainability assessment. The proposed framework integrates interpretable prediction, sustainability assessment, and multi-objective optimization to identify UHPC mixtures for prescribed strength targets, with experimental validation supporting practical mixture-design applications.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the global travel industry by enhancing personalization, operational efficiency, and strategic competitiveness. items.title: AI-Powered Predictive Women Safety Ecosystem with Real-Time Audio Threat Detection: A Review
items.abstract: Women's safety is still an everyday concern in public places, workplaces and homes, and most tools in use today depend on the victim pressing a button at the worst possible moment. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers another route: listening for distress in the surroundings, combining it with other signals, and forecasting where and when the risk is highest. This paper reviews 15 IEEE-published sources from 2014 to 2024 that relate to this idea. They cover IoT-based safety devices, scream and distress detection from audio, speech emotion and fear recognition, multimodal wearable systems, crime hotspot prediction, and edge and privacy-preserving deployment. The review finds that the audio models report accuracies between 92% and 100% on the datasets they were tested on, while the one multimodal wearable study that tested fear recognition on unseen subjects reached 63.61%. Crime-prediction methods are mature at city level but are rarely linked to women-specific incidents or to live sensing. Most studies rely on small, public or acted data, say little about false alarms, response delay and battery use, and give limited attention to privacy, accents and noisy streets. The paper contributes a comparison of eleven representative works, a conceptual seven-layer architecture that joins on-device audio detection with predictive risk analytics, and a prioritised list of research gaps. The architecture is conceptual and has not been tested experimentally.

items.title: An Analysis of Obstacles in Fulfilling Administrative Requirements for Marriage Registration by Prospective Brides and Grooms (A Case Study at the Office of Religious Affairs [KUA] in Tembalang, Semarang City)
items.abstract: This study aims to identify the obstacles faced by prospective couples in fulfilling the administrative requirements for marriage registration at the Tembalang Religious Affairs Office (KUA) in Semarang City, analyze the causal factors, and formulate appropriate solutions to overcome them. This research employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. Data were collected through interviews, questionnaires, and observation involving 7 KUA staff members and 20 prospective couples. Data analysis was conducted using a descriptive-analytical method based on the Miles and Huberman interactive model, strengthened by triangulation techniques. The findings reveal that the main obstacles include incomplete N1–N5 documents, birth certificates, health certificates, parents’ marriage books, outdated identity cards and family cards, commander’s permission for TNI/Polri members, and guardian-related issues due to parental divorce. Contributing factors include limited information, prospective couples’ lack of thoroughness, processes at other institutions, and family-related problems. In addition, the poorly positioned physical information media and non-ergonomic spatial layout exacerbate information asymmetry. This study recommends strengthening public education, improving spatial layout, and optimizing information media to enhance the effectiveness of marriage registration services.

items.title: An artificial intelligence meta-skills framework for undergraduate research
items.abstract: Undergraduate research faces unprecedented challenges in the digital era, as exponentially growing data increasingly shapes the university ecosystem. However, artificial intelligence, particularly tools such as ChatGPT, offers significant opportunities to address this transformation. Effective use requires advanced competencies in generating, acquiring, storing, and analyzing data. In response, this study developed and validated a new Big Data Socio-Technical Competence Scale to assess undergraduate students’ competencies in research contexts. This study examined the relationship between Big Data socio-technical competencies and undergraduate students' academic use of ChatGPT, as well as the underlying meta-skills for using AI in research. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design (QUAN → qual) was adopted, involving 418 undergraduate students. We used two measurement instruments: the newly developed and validated Big Data Socio-Technical Competence Scale and a scale measuring the academic use of ChatGPT; both showed high internal consistency, along with a semi-structured interview protocol. The findings show that Big Data competencies were generally low, whereas the academic use of ChatGPT for research was predominantly medium to high. Structural equation modeling revealed that socio-technical competencies in Big Data positively and significantly predict the academic use of ChatGPT (β = 0.269, p < .001). The qualitative phase identified nine Artificial Intelligence Meta-Skills for Undergraduate Research: (1) Critical Data Literacy, (2) Critical Thinking, (3) Epistemic Data Management, (4) Evidence-Based Decision-Making, (5) Critical Data Communication, (6) Metacognitive Regulation, (7) Emotional Self-Regulation, (8) Responsible Human–AI Agency, and (9) Ethical Reasoning. The study discusses educational implications and practical applications.

items.title: An Improved Model for Occupational Health and Safety Risk Assessment Based on Consensus Analysis and MARCOS Approach
items.abstract: Occupational health and safety risk assessment (OHSRA) is a critical activity to identify and analyze the risk of occupational hazards for ensuring the safety of workers, and then take measures to control occupational risk at a tolerable level. In this study, an improved OHSRA model based on consensus analysis and the measurement of alternatives and ranking according to compromise solution (MARCOS) method is introduced to assess and prioritize the risk of occupational hazards under linguistic D numbers (LDNs) environment. First, the LDNs are employed to express the uncertain or hesitant risk assessments of occupational hazards provided by experts. Second, an improved minimum conflict consensus method (MCCM) is adopted to coordinate the conflict opinions among experts considering their conflicting degrees. Then, the MARCOS method is modified to determine the risk ranking of occupational hazards. Finally, an illustrative hospital-based application focusing on medical staff occupational hazards is presented to show the implementation procedure of the proposed OHSRA model. Sensitivity and comparative analyses are further conducted to examine the robustness of the results within this specific application context.

items.title: An LLM-enabled decision support framework for rare-event financial risk screening in e-commerce logistics ecosystems
items.abstract: Purpose Rare financial-distress events create a distinctive decision-support problem in e-commerce logistics ecosystems: missing a distressed partner can be costly, yet excessive alerts can overwhelm limited human review capacity. This study investigates whether large language models (LLMs), when provided with mechanism-structured financial information, can support rare-event screening under extreme class imbalance. Design/methodology/approach Using Chinese A-share transportation and logistics firms as an empirical proxy for logistics-partner risk monitoring, we construct a two-year-ahead financial-distress prediction task containing 880 firm-year observations from feature years 2013–2022, including 12 ST/*ST cases. All conventional machine-learning (ML) models and eight zero-shot LLMs are evaluated on the same chronological holdout sample of 176 observations, including four distress cases. We develop Financial Narrative Serialization (FNS) to organize 21 financial and textual indicators into interpretable financial contexts and combine it with a Temporal Context-Aware Chain-of-Thought (TCA-CoT) protocol that structures the assessment around liquidity stress, inefficient expansion, and fundamental deterioration. ML benchmarks include unweighted learning, cost-sensitive learning, enhanced features, mechanism-feature ablation, and threshold sensitivity. Findings Extreme class imbalance produces markedly different screening behaviors across models. At a 0.5 reference threshold, the most selective cost-sensitive ML ensemble identifies two of four distress cases while generating three false positives; lower thresholds can recover additional distress cases but may eventually approach an all-alert rule. TCA-CoT increases recall for five of the eight LLMs and leaves recall unchanged for three. For Qwen-Turbo, recall rises from 0.50 to 1.00 as the number of flagged observations increases from 33 to 104. The additional false-positive observations exhibit, on average, weaker liquidity, higher leverage, poorer operating cash-flow quality, and lower profitability than true negatives. These results indicate that structured prompting can shift the LLM screening boundary toward financially vulnerable observations, although broader risk coverage increases the burden of secondary review. Practical implications The findings support a layered screening workflow in which AI prioritizes potentially vulnerable firms for subsequent human assessment. Model selection should therefore reflect the organization’s tolerance for missed risks and its available review capacity rather than rely on a single predictive metric. Originality/value This study develops a mechanism-structured financial representation for zero-shot LLM screening and evaluates ML and LLM approaches in a common rare-event environment. It further introduces a decision-support perspective that jointly considers distress coverage, false alarms, and human review volume.

items.title: An ODeL-based teacher professional development framework for teacher-facilitated human–AI collaboration in primary mathematics problem-solving: a conceptual analysis
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly present in primary mathematics classrooms, yet their educational value is widely argued to depend on how teachers use them. Existing models explain parts of this problem: AI-TPACK describes the knowledge teachers need, teacher-in-the-loop and human-centred AI models describe how control is shared between teachers and systems, and orchestration research describes how teachers coordinate classroom activity. What remains under-theorised is the pathway linking the way open distance e-learning (ODeL) professional development builds teachers’ capacity to its enactment when AI scaffolds learners’ problem-solving. This conceptual article asks: through which mechanisms, and under which conditions, can ODeL-based professional development be expected to enable teacher-facilitated human–AI collaboration that supports primary learners’ mathematical problem-solving? The analysis combined an integrative review of peer-reviewed and selected grey literature with theory synthesis: sources were identified through structured database searches, screened against pre-specified criteria, coded for constructs, mechanisms and boundary conditions, and organised by level of analysis. The primary context is South African primary schooling (Grades 1–7) and low-bandwidth, predominantly asynchronous ODeL. Positioning four perspectives within a multilevel meta-model, Intelligent-TPACK at the teacher level, Zone of Proximal Development scaffolding and social constructivism at the interaction and classroom levels, and Polya’s heuristic as an analytic lens at the learner level, with transactional distance theory at the programme level, I propose a three-layer framework that distinguishes inputs, mechanisms, practices and outcomes, and derive seven testable propositions. These include teacher orchestration as a mediator between AI-TPACK and scaffolding quality; infrastructure readiness, learner age, language, and AI type as moderators; and governance and children’s rights as cross-cutting boundary conditions. Unlike models that specify teacher knowledge or the division of control alone, the framework specifies the professional development pathway through which human–AI collaboration is expected to benefit learners. I propose that well-designed ODeL professional development is an enabling condition for such benefit, not a guarantee of it, and close with implementation and evaluation indicators for teacher educators, policymakers, school leaders, researchers and learners.

items.title: Application of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Methods to Optimize Energy System Stability
items.abstract: This article presents a systematic analysis of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods applied to the optimization of energy system stability. Deep learning architectures for forecasting electricity demand and renewable energy generation, reinforcement learning algorithms for microgrid control, the concept of digital twins, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods are examined. The application of hybrid models reduces forecasting errors by 20–35% over ultra-short-term forecasting horizons ranging from several minutes to several hours. The transition to probabilistic forecasting reduces balancing costs by 8–15%, while the use of digital twins decreases operating costs by 15–25%. Current challenges limiting the implementation of intelligent technologies in the energy sector are identified, and priority areas for further research are outlined. The results are systematized in comparative tables suitable for practical use when selecting appropriate methodological tools.

items.title: Application of dynamic symbolic execution and test coverage enhancement combined with artificial intelligence in large-scale web software systems
items.abstract: Aiming at the bottleneck problems of path explosion and low efficiency of constraint solving faced by dynamic symbolic execution (DSE) in large-scale Web software systems, this paper applies a DSE and test coverage enhancement method combined with artificial intelligence (AI). Firstly, an Actor-Critic dual network model is constructed based on the PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) algorithm. The Actor network outputs the probability distribution of path selection, and the Critic network evaluates the value of path state. Secondly, the path priority sorting strategy is updated through the generalized advantage estimation and pruning mechanism, and the path depth threshold is gradually increased by combining curriculum learning. The key branch priority solving strategy is applied to optimize the efficiency of constraint solving. Finally, after each round of symbolic execution, the coverage increment is used as a reward signal to update the model parameters online and dynamically optimize the path exploration strategy. Experimental results show that this method significantly improves the efficiency of path exploration (the number of paths reaches 225 and 216, respectively) and test coverage (74.9% and 73.4%) on large-scale Web systems, with an average solution success rate of 79.8% and an average vulnerability detection rate of 88%. It has good vulnerability detection capabilities and resource adaptability, and provides an efficient and scalable new paradigm for automated testing of complex systems.

items.title: Applications of Generative Artificial Intelligence Teaching in Nursing Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
items.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in nursing education. Its educational effects in nursing remain uncertain. Purpose: To evaluate the effects of using GenAI in teaching nursing. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception to July 2026. Standardized mean differences and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were pooled using random-effects models. Heterogeneity, sensitivity analyses, meta-regression, and small-study effects were explored. Results: Seventeen studies involving 1456 participants were included. GenAI-integrated teaching was associated with higher knowledge scores (standardized mean differences 0.53, 95% CI 0.03-1.04), practice-related scores (SMD 1.25, 95% CI 0.23-2.28), and teaching satisfaction (SMD 0.58, 95% CI 0.02-1.13). Attitudes, competency, and self-efficacy did not differ significantly. Meta-regression findings were exploratory. Conclusions: GenAI-integrated teaching may improve knowledge, practice-related performance, and satisfaction in nursing education. However, extreme heterogeneity and sensitivity to individual studies limit confidence in the magnitude and reproducibility of these effects. GenAI should be used as a supervised pedagogical adjunct pending high-quality trials.

items.title: ARMS 2026: UTS TeamBuilder: AI and data driven insights for building cross-university collaboration
items.abstract: Universities have a wide range of expertise, but identifying the right people for complex, cross-disciplinary opportunities can be difficult. Expertise is often spread across faculties, research centres and different institutional systems. When funding and partnership opportunities have short response periods, those supporting team formation may rely on familiar networks and people with relevant but less obvious capabilities. UTS TeamBuilder is an AI-assisted tool that helps people find the right researchers, explore expertise across the university, and form teams around new opportunities. Rather than simply producing a list of names, the tool supports the broader team formation process, from framing the challenge and exploring institutional capability to preparing introductions and facilitating early conversations. The tool brings together evidence from multiple institutional sources, including researcher profiles, publication abstracts, research projects, proposals and staff bios. It uses natural language processing, network analysis, interactive visualization and generative AI to help users explore expertise, assess possible team combinations, and understand the evidence behind suggestions. Outputs can include expertise landscapes, preliminary team propositions, personalised invitations and prompts to support early team conversations. A key principle behind the tool is that AI should support, rather than replace, human judgement. Users can inspect the visualizations and analysis used by the AI, refine the researcher pool, explore proposed team members, and adjust the direction of the analysis. TeamBuilder therefore broadens the user’s field of view and provides informed starting points, while leaving decisions about team composition and suitability with the human user.

items.abstract: This chapter offers an overview of widely used artificial intelligence terminology to support informed engagement in art therapy. As AI systems evolve rapidly, ongoing AI literacy combined with digital humility helps practitioners, students, and educators evaluate emerging tools in ways that align with professional ethics. The chapter defines core concepts such as artificial intelligence, large language models, chatbot, agent, and deep learning, alongside evolving social and policy terms including AI slop and responsible AI. It situates these terms within art therapy practice and broader societal contexts. The chapter underscores that AI systems are computational tools with significant transformative capacity and therefore require ethical discernment. Their outputs differ fundamentally from human creativity and lived experience and must be approached with careful clinical judgment, reflective practice, and professional accountability.

items.title: Artificial intelligence across the stone-associated urinary infection pathway: imaging, urosepsis prediction, and antimicrobial stewardship
items.abstract: Abstract Complicated urinary tract infection associated with urinary stone disease remains clinically challenging because obstruction, infected stones, delayed microbiological confirmation, and antimicrobial resistance may converge in the same patient. Artificial intelligence can support this pathway when it is framed as clinical risk integration rather than isolated image recognition. We conducted a structured narrative search of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from database inception to 31 July 2026, supplemented by reference chaining and relevant clinical and reporting guidelines. The synthesis distinguishes direct evidence in stone-associated infection and perioperative infectious outcomes from indirect evidence in stone detection, volumetry, recurrence, and general UTI stewardship. Radiomics and machine learning studies show promising discrimination, but the evidence remains predominantly retrospective and frequently lacks external validation, complete calibration reporting, and prospective impact assessment. Artificial intelligence should therefore be treated as an adjunct to urological assessment, cultures, imaging, antimicrobial stewardship, and timely source control. For African settings, pragmatic validation must account for local resistance patterns, uneven access to CT and microbiology, referral delays, infrastructure, and the availability of urgent drainage.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and digital transformation for sustainable supply chain performance
items.abstract: This study examines the nexus between digital technology adoption and Sustainable Supply Chain Management, focusing on their combined impact on sustainability performance. By bridging the domains of digital transformation and sustainability, the research advances a comprehensive conceptual framework that captures the effects of Industry 4.0 technologies, specifically the Internet of Things, artificial intelligence, and blockchain, on sustainable supply chain outcomes. The proposed model posits that digital technology adoption enhances sustainability performance indirectly through improved supply chain transparency, with this relationship moderated by the presence of a skilled workforce. Grounded in a thorough review of contemporary literature, the study highlights the role of Industry 4.0 technologies in promoting eco-efficient production and logistics, the contribution of blockchain to strengthening transparency, and the optimization of resource utilization through AI. An empirical quantitative study based on survey data collected from 250 manufacturing firms provides evidence of the partial mediation effect of transparency and validates the moderating influence of human capital in reinforcing the relationship between digital transformation and sustainability. The findings offer novel theoretical insights into the mechanisms linking digital adoption to SSCM and yield practical implications for managers seeking to leverage Industry 4.0 technologies for sustainability objectives. The paper concludes by outlining directions for future research to further advance the digital–sustainability interface.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and doctrinal authority: Emerging ethical and theological questions for the Church in Ghana
items.abstract: This study examined the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and doctrinal authority in the context of the Church of Ghana. The increasing use of AI in sermon preparation, biblical interpretation, theological research, and religious communication has raised important theological and ethical concerns regarding the integrity of Christian doctrine and the legitimacy of machine-assisted theological content. The study specifically explored how AI influences theological interpretation, the ethical issues associated with AI-generated religious content, and how churches should respond to AI-driven theological tools. The study was underpinned by Hermeneutical Theory and Technological Determinism Theory and grounded in the interpretivist paradigm. It used a qualitative research approach with a phenomenological research design. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with nineteen purposively selected participants, including pastors, church leaders, seminary lecturers, theological educators, and theological students. The data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed that AI is increasingly being used in sermon structuring, biblical explanation, theological research, contextual communication, and comparative doctrinal synthesis. However, the study also found that AI-generated religious content raises serious concerns related to doctrinal inconsistency, authorship and authenticity, overdependence, misinformation, and spiritual disconnection. The study concludes that while AI may serve as a useful assistive tool in ministry and theological education, it cannot function as a source of doctrinal authority. The paper recommends doctrinal oversight, digital theological literacy, and ethical guidelines for the use of responsible AI in Christian contexts.
